outcome: No source establishes any change to whether unknot recognition is in P. Marc Lackenby's 2021 quasi-polynomial-time algorithm remains an unpublished announcement with no arXiv preprint found and, per multiple 2025-era sources, still not in the peer-reviewed literature. AI/ML work found in the window (a Google DeepMind/Oxford reinforcement-learning paper and a follow-up RL paper) targets the unknotting number and hard unknot diagrams, a related but distinct question, not the polynomial-time recognition question stated in this bullet.
summary: The bullet asks specifically whether unknots can be recognized in polynomial time — i.e., whether unknot recognition is in P. Nothing found in the 26 January 2024–22 September 2026 window changes the status of that question. Lackenby's 2021 announcement of a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm (n^{c log n} steps) predates the window and, per the Oxford Mathematical Institute page and searches run for this record, remains unpublished with no arXiv preprint located as of the check date; it would not settle the P question even if published, since quasi-polynomial time is weaker than polynomial time. A 2026 arXiv paper on incompressible surfaces, hierarchies and unknot recognition (2607.23350) gives a new proof of the already-known NP membership result via a different route, not new progress on P-membership. Two machine-learning papers turned up repeatedly in searches: (1) 'The unknotting number, hard unknot diagrams, and reinforcement learning' (arXiv:2409.09032, submitted 13 September 2024, authors including Applebaum, Blackwell, Davies, Edlich, Juhász, Lackenby, Tomašev, Zheng — a Google DeepMind/Oxford collaboration), which uses an RL agent to find minimal unknotting-crossing-change sequences and determine unknotting numbers for many knots; and (2) a March 2026 follow-up, 'RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number' (arXiv:2603.07955, Dranowski/Kabkov/Tubbenhauer), which extends this with a self-improving RL pipeline for Reidemeister-move simplification. Both are squarely about the unknotting number (minimum crossing changes to reach the unknot) and about heuristic diagram simplification, not about the computational-complexity question of whether recognizing an unknot diagram as trivial can be decided in polynomial time. Per the scope rule (§3.1), a different question about the same objects is a related problem, not a case of this one, so these do not count as movement on this bullet even though they are squarely 'about unknots' and do involve AI. A separate, unrelated 2025 result (Brittenham and Hermiller, arXiv preprint posted ~June 2025, digested in Quanta Magazine 22 September 2025) disproved the long-standing additivity conjecture for unknotting numbers under connected sum — again the unknotting-number question, not recognition complexity, and involves no AI. The 2020 'Learning to Unknot' paper (arXiv:2010.16263, Gukov et al., CALT-2020-046/CERN-TH-2020-179) that keeps surfacing in searches predates the window (submitted 28 October 2020) and is itself a heuristic ML classifier/RL-move-finder, not a complexity proof, so it is out of scope on both counts. No source found claims, disputes, or withdraws any polynomial-time algorithm for unknot recognition in this window; the honest answer is that the problem is unchanged and open.
competing_reading: One could argue the DeepMind/Oxford RL papers on hard unknot diagrams are close enough to count as 'progress' on unknot recognition broadly, since they do produce practical algorithms that recognize (and prove) unknottedness for large classes of hard diagrams via explicit Reidemeister/crossing-change sequences, and Lackenby himself is a co-author bridging both the complexity work and the ML work. If the bullet were read loosely as 'progress on algorithmically recognizing unknots' rather than strictly 'is the decision problem in P', these papers would be `progress` with `ai_role` `assisted` or `bound`. I did not adopt this reading because the papers' own framing and results are about the unknotting number and empirical/heuristic performance on specific diagram classes (up to 200 crossings, or engineered 'very hard' unknots), not about worst-case polynomial-time bounds or the complexity class P, which is what the Wikipedia bullet asks.
what_would_settle_it: A peer-reviewed publication or well-digested preprint proving (or disproving) a worst-case polynomial-time upper bound for the general unknot recognition decision problem — as opposed to a quasi-polynomial bound, a heuristic/empirical algorithm, or a result about a different quantity such as the unknotting number.
